newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia takes slower path on car tariff cuts.
newsitem.headline: Australia takes slower path on car tariff cuts.

text.p: Australia, fighting chronic unemployment and a manufacturing industry recession, on Thursday slowed its pace of car tariff cuts, but said it remained committed to an ambitious Asia-Pacific free trade pact.

Prime Minister John Howard said car import tariffs would be frozen at 15 percent from 2000 and cut to 10 percent in January 2005, rejecting more dramatic cuts urged by his chief industry advisory group, the Productivity Commission.
Carmakers immediately welcomed the plan -- which will be reviewed again in 2005 -- as a sensible measure creating stability for their future investment and saving jobs.
Howard said his plan was a balanced decision that met international trade obligations and also protected jobs and a valuable domestic industry.

"It recognises our trade obligations, it's consistent with our APEC (Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum) goals and it also recognises the desirability of providing investment certainty and investment predictability," he told reporters at a joint news conference with industry chiefs.

The government will also introduce an export assistance scheme for the automotive industry, to run until 2005 from the expiration of an existing programme in 2000. Howard did not detail the new scheme, but said it would meet world trade rules.
Howard also said he would establish an automotive trade council, appoint a special auto trade negotiator and set up a A$20 million (US$15 million), four-year market access programme.
Car tariffs are due to fall to 15 percent by 2000 from 22.5 percent under plans already in place and the Productivity Commission had urged further cuts to five percent by 2005.
Unions, the Labor opposition and state governments warned that would cost thousands of jobs, adding to the nation's already high unemployment rate which is stuck above 8.5 percent.
Australia's four carmakers -- two American and two Japanese -- all warned the commission's plan threatened their survival in the tough Australian market.
Car industry chiefs said the Howard plan would now let them invest with confidence and avoid job losses.
"This ... gives us the opportunity to go ahead and invest in the country and should certainly avoid job losses as such," Ford Australia managing director David Morgan said.
Ford Motor Co and three other companies -- Mitsubishi Motors, General Motors Corp and Toyota Motor Corp -- have manufacturing plants in Australia.
"We believe it (the Howard plan) gives us the opportunity to go on and invest with confidence in the new models," said Mitsubishi managing director Mike Quinn.
Howard said he remained committed to obligations to cut trade barriers to zero by 2010 under the APEC free trade pact.

But he said the APEC target did not lay down specific strategies for specific industries. The 18-member APEC pact calls for developed members such as Australia to cut barriers by 2010 and for developing nations to do so by 2020.
